Financial planning · Advice and costs · Visual planning guide

Where Canadians seek financial advice, and how to budget for the service

Four charts pair selected official survey observations with a separate, editable comparison of an initial planning project, periodic reviews and an annual retainer.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Keep the survey context separate from a hypothetical advice-fee budget

Interactive planning lab

Nominal fees: initial project and scheduled reviews$3,191.23
Nominal fees: annual retainer$19,709.5
Present cost: retainer minus project schedule$14,318.49

The first two charts reproduce selected 2024 survey observations from the FCAC spotlight issued 17 November 2025 and modified 21 November 2025, retrieved 25 October 2026. They describe reported source use, not advisor quality or the effect of obtaining advice. The other two charts are separate hypothetical fee schedules. Both start immediately. The project path pays the initial fee at time zero, then a review after every selected number of complete years, only if its payment date falls before the end of the selected service window. The retainer path pays at the start of every service year. Future review and retainer quotes grow at the selected annual rate; the initial project fee is paid once without escalation. The discount rate converts dated payments to starting-date present cost and is not an expected portfolio return. No household funding account, investment performance, taxes, reimbursement, product costs or service outcomes are calculated. The two packages are not assumed to provide equivalent services.

The central idea

Survey popularity does not measure advice quality. Define the service you need, verify its scope and price, and draw the payment calendar before judging the cost.

01

Use the survey to understand reported behaviour

FCAC’s advice spotlight reports professional-advisor use of 20% among people aged 18–34, 26% among those aged 35–54, and 27% among those aged 55 or older. Its data come from the 2024 Canadian Financial Capability Survey. The spotlight was issued on 17 November 2025 and modified on 21 November; the observations remain tied to the survey period.

The first chart uses a different denominator for each age group. Adding the percentages would not produce a national share. The gaps describe reported use; the displayed source does not supply uncertainty intervals for these comparisons, and this guide makes no significance or causal claim.

The second chart selects three sources among the 18–34 group: family or friends, professional advisors and social media. People can use more than one channel, and other channels are omitted. The bars are therefore not a complete allocation of one common pool. A pie chart would suggest a partition that these selected figures do not establish.

02

Define the work before comparing a fee

A statement about where people obtain advice does not tell you whether an individual source can answer your specific question. A tax calculation, an investment implementation task and an ongoing household plan can require different work and qualifications.

FCAC’s guidance on choosing an advisor recommends examining the services, cost, compensation and relevant experience. For a real engagement, clarify the deliverables, the assumptions to be reviewed, who performs the work and which follow-up is included. Check the current qualifications and applicable authorizations for the actual services needed.

The calculator below assumes two hypothetical fee packages. It does not assume that their services are equivalent, that one arrangement produces better outcomes, or that a survey respondent used either package. The figures are entered prices for a budgeting exercise, not evidence of typical Canadian fees.

03

An initial project and an annual retainer have different dates

The project schedule pays one initial planning fee immediately. It then pays a separate review fee after each selected number of complete years, provided that payment falls inside the chosen service window. The annual-retainer schedule pays at the start of every service year, including an immediate first payment.

In the original example, the initial project costs CAD 1,500. A CAD 500 review in starting-date dollars is scheduled every three years, and the competing first annual retainer is CAD 1,800. Future quoted review and retainer fees increase at an assumed 2% per year.

A review after three years is paid at time three, the start of service year four. A window containing only the first three service years does not include that later payment. Over ten service years, the original project schedule includes reviews at times three, six and nine, with nominal amounts of approximately CAD 530.60, CAD 563.08 and CAD 597.55.

The annual-fee chart connects the amounts charged at successive year starts. The connecting line is a reading aid; it does not add charges between those payment dates.

04

Keep total cash outlay separate from the value of payment timing

The final chart accumulates the nominal fees. In the original ten-year example, the project and scheduled reviews total approximately CAD 3,191.23. The growing annual retainer totals approximately CAD 19,709.50. Both totals include their immediate first payment.

The present-cost metric answers a different question. It discounts each dated payment back to the start using the selected effective annual discount assumption. A payment at time t has present cost payment ÷ (1 + discount rate)t. An immediate payment has t = 0 and is not discounted.

At the original 3% discount assumption, the present costs are approximately CAD 2,915.12 and CAD 17,233.61, a difference of CAD 14,318.49. These are timing calculations, not investment returns or the value of advice. A higher nominal total paid over many years need not have the same present cost as the same nominal amount paid immediately.

The discount input is independent of the fee-growth assumption. Setting it equal to fee growth makes every annual-retainer payment have the same starting-date present cost under this model; that is an arithmetic identity, not a forecast about prices or markets.

05

Use the cost schedule as one part of a service decision

Before implementing a fee budget, obtain the actual terms. A quote may exclude implementation, additional meetings, specialized work, sales tax, investment-product expenses or a change in circumstances. An annual arrangement may include services that a one-time project does not, and the reverse can also be true.

The tool calculates neither the cash available to pay the bill nor any benefit from the service. A low total does not establish that a plan can be implemented or maintained; a high total does not establish that the work creates enough value. Service scope, competence, incentives and the ability to act on recommendations need their own review.

  1. Write the question or decision for which help is needed.
  2. Confirm the deliverables and the relevant expertise.
  3. List the initial, recurring and event-triggered charges separately.
  4. Place each charge at its payment date and budget the cash.
  5. Review the arrangement when circumstances or the work required change.

The survey panels provide context for how people report seeking help. The fee panels provide an inspectable cost calendar. Keeping those roles separate allows the article to explain both without treating popularity as a quality score or a quoted fee as a promised financial result.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first two charts show selected 2024 Canadian Financial Capability Survey observations reported by FCAC. The other two are independent hypothetical fee schedules. Survey use, service quality and modeled cost are different measurements. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FCAC · Spotlight on Canadians’ use of financial advice ↗

    Selected 2024 source-use observations. Issued 17 November 2025; modified 21 November 2025; retrieved 25 October 2026. The stored extract preserves six age/source values and the original HTML SHA-256.

  2. FCAC · Survey findings on seeking financial advice ↗

    News release dated 17 November 2025. Independently corroborates the three selected younger-adult source shares and the February–March 2024 survey period.

  3. FCAC · Choosing a financial advisor ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026. Supports examining the work, relevant qualifications, costs and compensation. No quote, advisor ranking or service-value estimate is reproduced here.
